clean.tl: Flour tins, big cases of meat , wow, they gave to him for nothing, they gave them to Sarak.

clean.tx: Amerika kereremik naeya ikiwep wia urufikua.
clean.tl: The Americans have arrived, so let’s go and see them.
When he went to Ulingan they gave him a bomb
“Blast fish with this bomb bombs,” they told him.

clean.tx: Maa enowa iwemik, palauwa dram, bata tin naap nain, ne rais weetak.
clean.tl: They gave him food, flour drums, and things like butter tins, but no rice.

clean.tx: Ne irakowa weesereya i owowa oromik.
clean.tl: And when the war ended we came down to the village.

clean.tx: Irakowa fa, opaimika eeya akena yaa, kamenap aakuniyen yaa?
clean.tl: Oh the war - the talk lasts very long - how can we talk about it?

clean.tx: Aakuniyen, aakuniyen, me pepek, me welawiyen.
clean.tl: We will talk and talk, but it is not enough, we won’t finish it.

clean.tx: Yo yena yaiya Tup ifa kuok nain opaimika maiyem.
clean.tl: I tell a story about that when my uncle Tup was bitten by a snake.
He went up and eastwards.

clean.tx: Ekap umukinen naep onamikeya ifa kerawak, mamepaperuma gelegelemutitik nain
clean.tl: He went eastwards and when he was trying to extinguish the fire a snake bit him, the very small death adder.

clean.tx: Keraweya, aria nomokowa gelemuta puukap ifa makena nain ifakimok.
clean.tl: It bit him, and he cut a small tree and killed the snake.
He killed it and hung it on a tree branch.
He hung it and came down, he came down to the village.
He came down to the village and was hungry and roasted bananas.

clean.tx: Akia ikep enemikok, ifa marasin nain kema wiar iwak.
clean.tl: He roasted bananas and when he was eating them the snake poison entered his liver.

clean.tx: Ne auwa ame wia maakeya res aawep merena ifa kerawak nain puukamik.
clean.tl: And when he told my father and others, they took a razor and made a cut into the leg that the snake had bitten.
They made a cut and put medicine into it.
They put medicine but no .
The snake poison was already strong.

clean.tx: Ne akia ikek nain me enek.
clean.tl: And he didn’t eat the bananas that he roasted.

clean.tx: Nan mukuna ikeya o nan samor aawok.
clean.tl: They were there on the fire and he really got bad there.
He felt dizzy.

clean.tx: Epa naap kokomareya o lawisiw samor aawok.
clean.tl: When it got dark he became worse.

clean.tx: Ne haussik peku naep miiwaasa nopamik.
clean.tl: And they looked for a vehicle to take him to the aidpost.

clean.tx: Miiwaasa nopap, iiriw Naawura miiwaasa awona nain wiar aawemik.
clean.tl: They looked for a vehicle and got Naawura’s earlier old vehicle
They got it and took him to the aidpost.

clean.tx: Ne kiiriw nan Medebur ekamik, mua napuma onaiya.
clean.tl: And again from there they went to Medebur, with the sick man.

clean.tx: Ekap Medebur neeke ikemika kaikowa mua nain nopamik, imenap maakiwkin o miimok.
clean.tl: They went and there in Medebur they searched for the health officer, and when they found him and told him he went ahead of them .

clean.tx: Aria, wi kiiriw neeke miiwaasa umok.
clean.tl: Alright, again when they were there the truck broke down.

clean.tx: Miiwaasa umeya miiwaasa nain onamikaiwkin epa kokomarek, epa iimeka tuunek.
clean.tl: The truck broke down and while they were working on the truck it became dark, it became past midnight.

clean.tx: Ne kiiriw miiwaasa nan ikeya mua nain nabena suuwamik.
clean.tl: And again the truck stayed there and they carried the man on a carrying pole.

clean.tx: Saapara nan suusa iwemik, wiena ifa suusa nain.
clean.tl: There in Saapara they gave him an injection, that snake injection of theirs.
They gave him that but no, it was not enough.
And they stayed there.
They stayed and stayed there and there he died.
There he died and they just carried him on their shouders.

clean.tx: Miiwaasa samorareya oram akua aawep ekapemik.
clean.tl: The truck was broken and they just carried him on their shoulders and came.
They carried him on their shoulders and as they were coming he got very heavy.
He got heavy and so Kuuten and others walked ahead.

clean.tx: Miimep ekapep owow mua wia maakemik.
clean.tl: They came ahead and told the village people.

clean.tx: Ne owow mua wia aawep kiiriw kiremik.
clean.tl: And they got village men and turned back again.

clean.tx: Miiwaasa awona nain miiwaasa faowa mua neeke wia aawok.
clean.tl: The driver of that old truck took them from there.
He took them from there and they came.

clean.tx: Epap ona koora inawap naap arewap pokap ikemik.
clean.tl: They came and laid him in his house and they sat and waited like that.
As we were waiting it dawned.
But no.
We talked to the owners of the Malala truck.

clean.tx: Miiwaasa wia maakep, ekapeya, kes onomamik.
clean.tl: We talked to them about the truck and when it came we made a coffin for him.
We put him inside the coffin and took him .
We took him and buried him in Bogia.

clean.tx: Bogia nan wuap i kiiriw ekapemik.
clean.tl: We buried him in Bogia and came back again.
We came and arrived in the village at night.
The talk is just like that, finished.

clean.tx: Yo aakisa opaimika mainen, pon aawem nain.
clean.tl: I will now tell a story about that when I caught a turtle.

clean.tx: Yo uura arua isimap aasa karuemiawikok pon sisina ikeya, piipa unowa soomaremikeya mikam.
clean.tl: At night I lighted a lantern and was paddling in the canoe and I saw a turtle in the shallow water, walking among a lot of seaweed, and I speared it.

clean.tx: Mikap, patot mikap, aawep, aasa wuap, amapurupep, yena koora wuap, uuriw epa wiimeya orop, saa paep uupemik.
clean.tl: I speared it, speared it with a fishing spear, took it, put it in the canoe, brought it up , put it in my house, in the morning when it dawned went down and butchered it on the beach and we cooked it.

clean.tx: Uupep weesereya, aria oposia gelemuta wiam erup fain wia wuomam.
clean.tl: When the cooking was finished, alright I put a little for these two .
And now I speak it on a tape recorder.

clean.tx: Ne yo efa maakiwkin yo aakisa tep maem.
clean.tl: And they told me and now I spoke it on a taperecorder.
My speech is there.

clean.tx: Mera aawowa sira e era wapen inawiya okaiwi kuisow.
clean.tl: There are six ways to do fishing.

clean.tx: Kaul aawimik, arua karuimik, maer puukimik, patopat mera urumimik, oko galasimimik.
clean.tl: They catch them with hooks, fish with torches, hit the surface, search the fish with fishing spears and dive with goggles.
Another is a fishtrap.

clean.tx: Oko sisina ifemakimik, oko malol ifemakimik.
clean.tl: One is that they let it down in the shallow water, the other is that they let it down in the deep sea.

clean.tx: Ne sisina nain me yoowa akena.
clean.tl: the shallow water is not very hard.
Oh the deep sea is a bit hard.

clean.tx: Sisina nain, soo ika oninan, soo ika kaikap otal opora ifemakinan.
clean.tl: As for the shallow water , you make a stand for the fistrap, tie the trap to the stand and let it down at the mouth of the reef.

clean.tx: Ifemakep nomona iinan wuainan, ikoka ifera me pikiwowa nain.
clean.tl: You let it down and then put stones on top of it, so that later the sea won’t take it away.

clean.tx: Soo nain ona malin saana ifemakimik.
clean.tl: The fishtrap is let down during the calm season.
Not during the stormy time.

clean.tx: Aria malol ifemakimik nain aana puukimik, makera unowa puukap makera nain anetirimik.
clean.tl: Alright the one that is let down in the deep sea , they cut cane, and after cutting a lot of makera cane, tie the canes .

clean.tx: Anetirikiwep urufimik, makera nain maaya pepek.
clean.tl: They keep tying them and then see that the cane is long enough.

clean.tx: Aria makera miirifa okaiwi soo kaikimik, okaiwi pia kaikimik, piakina naimik nain.
clean.tl: Alright one end of the cane is tied to the trap, to the other end they tie a bamboo called piakina.

clean.tx: Ne soo ifemakowa epa aasa suuwimik.
clean.tl: And at the time of letting the trap down they push the canoe out.

clean.tx: Aasa suuwap soo aasa iinan wuap poraimik.
clean.tl: They push the canoe out and put the trap on top of the canoe and take it down .
They go down and at the deep sea they throw the fishtrap down.
They throw it and hold on to the cane.
They hold it and let go a little.
When it has gone down and sits on the sand they will let go of it.

clean.tx: Ne soo nainiw mufowa pun naap, aana neeke mufimik.
clean.tl: And the pulling of the fishtrap is like that too, it is pulled by the cane there.

clean.tx: Aana neeke mufep, purupep aasa wuaimik.
clean.tl: They pull it by the cane there, bring it up and put it in the canoe.

clean.tx: Aasa wuap, mera aawep weesereya nainiw fuurkimik.
clean.tl: They put it in the canoe, get the fish and when that is finished they throw it down again.
That is the fishtrap way.
Alright is like that too.

clean.tx: Wi emeria kaalalimik, kaalalep orop otal maer arimik.
clean.tl: The women wade, they wade down and at the reef they start the surface-hitting.
They start hitting the surface and keep coming up towards the shore.

clean.tx: Pona neeke mera nomona ona iwomakeya, wi wapen ona nain suuwimik.
clean.tl: When they have reached the shore, a lot of fish have entered holes in the reef and they push their hands in the holes .

clean.tx: Ne mua patopat aawep saa iimarep ikaikuan.
clean.tl: And the men will take the fishing spears and be standing on the beach.
When the fish comes up to the shallow water they will spear it with a fishing spear.
And another is diving with goggles.

clean.tx: Nain iiriw me kererek, aakisa fan.
clean.tl: That didn’t come up in the old days, just recently.

clean.tx: Wiena galasimowa amia onimik, onap galasimimik.
clean.tl: They make their own fishing guns, and having made them they fish diving with goggles.
And another : they watch for fish with a fishing spear.

clean.tx: Nain ona mua taraka nain mera mikinan, patopat opowa nain.
clean.tl: If you are an accurate man, you will spear the fish, holding the spear.

clean.tx: O mua naap nain ikoka uferinan.
clean.tl: A man with poor aim will miss.
And another : they do torch-fishing.
They light lamps and do torch-fishing.

clean.tx: Parina isimap afukarep, nain ona kak saana
clean.tl: They light lamps and do torch-fishing and – that in the flying fish season.

clean.tx: Kak saana wi parina isimap orop kak isakimik.
clean.tl: In the flying fish season they light lamps and go down and spear flying fish.
Flying fish, longtom and other fish.
They spear small dussumier’s garfish, kookari fish, those.

clean.tx: Ne kak saana kak oraimik, ne parina ona wakesimowa onaiya ikaiya.
clean.tl: And in the flying fish season they go down for flying fish, and the lamp has a covering.

clean.tx: Ikoka wakesimeya mera mamaiya ekapinon, aasa mamaiya.
clean.tl: Later when you cover it the fish will come close, close to the canoe.

clean.tx: Aasa mamaiya ekapeya aria parina kiiriw mauwa one.
clean.tl: When they come close to the canoe, then again do what .
Do that and spear the fish.
When you have finished spearing them you will cover it again.
That is how they fish with a lamp.
Alright another way is throwing the hook.

clean.tx: Kumin wiimep, uuriw orop kaul wafurimik, aasa suuwap, o papako uura.
clean.tl: They gather hermit crabs and go down in the morning and throw the hook, having pushed the canoe out – or some at night.

clean.tx: Kaul wafurowa maa eneka, ona mera maa eneka, kumin, wutkekela, ne mera gelemutitik, nain kaul wafurimik.
clean.tl: Fish-throwing bait, fish-bait, hermit crabs, calamari and small fish – with those they throw the hook.

clean.tx: Ne emeria wiena pona iimarep kaul wafurimik, ifer pona
clean.tl: And the women themselves stand on the shore and throw the hook, on the seashore.

clean.tx: O mua aasa suuwap kaul wafurimik.
clean.tl: The men push the canoe and throw the hook .

clean.tx: Ne kaul wafurowa mera aawowa eliw, maa marew.
clean.tl: And the hook-throwing is a good way to get fish, there is nothing to it.
Diving with goggles is a bit hard.

clean.tx: Kemawisa pukinan, mua bug maaya nain eliw mera unowa isakinon, mua bug iiwa nain weetak.
clean.tl: You will be out of breath, a man with big lungs will spear many fish, a man with small lungs won’t.
Fishtrap is good.
Now I tell a little story.

clean.tx: Manina nan koka iwamik, pika ifara mufowa naep.
clean.tl: From the garden there they went to the jungle to pull vines for the fence.

clean.tx: Pika ifara mufewiawikok ifa maneka siowa wiar aawo
clean.tl: When he was moving around pulling the vines, a big snake grabbed his dog.
As he was killing it, the snake released the dog.
The snake released the dog and fled.
They ran away and came down to the village.
The talk is there, it is finished.

clean.tx: Tunde fikera kuumiwkin ikiwep waaya mikam nain maiyem.
clean.tl: I tell about that when on Tuesday they burned kunai grass and I went and speared a pig.

clean.tx: Tunde uuriw kiikir akena iwera fookap ikiwemik.
clean.tl: On Tuesday morning we split a coconut and went.

clean.tx: Ne iwera fookowa garanga nain wiena owow ara wiar ikua, ne fikera pun wiena nain
clean.tl: And the coconut splitting was in that family’s section of the village, and the kunai grass was theirs too.
They cooked food in the coconut splitting place.
We ate and held a coconut and split it.

clean.tx: Nain weesereya woowa akua aawep ikiwemik.
clean.tl: When that was finished, we carried spears on our shoulders and went.

clean.tx: Ikiwep fikera onaiya nan pokap, wi yapen mua unow pokap, nainiw neeke iwera fookamik, maa enemik.
clean.tl: We went and sat down there among the kunai grass, we sat down together with the inland men, and again there we split a coconut and ate food.

clean.tx: Weesereya ama kuisow naap mukuna enekamik.
clean.tl: When that was finished at about one o’clock the fire was lighted.
The fire was first lighted at the top

clean.tx: Neeke aweoromik i fiker saakia or fikera epia ookamik.
clean.tl: From there it was burning down and we went down the ashes and followed the grass fire.

clean.tx: Ookap orop ema mamaiya waaya gelemuta urupok.
clean.tl: We followed it down and near the hill a small pig came up.
It was not big, it was a small light-coloured piglet.

clean.tx: Mua arow akena epa nain iimaremik, yos erepam.
clean.tl: Exactly three men stood at that place, I was the fourth.

clean.tx: Waaya gelemuta nain urupemikeya mua arow naap uferamik.
clean.tl: When the small pig was coming up those three men missed it.
When they missed it and it was coming up I speared it.
I speared it and called my spirit name.

clean.tx: No inasina unuma me unufinan mua oko waaya nain mik nefar aawinon.
clean.tl: If you do not call spirit name, another man will spear that pig and take it from you.

clean.tx: Nain opora marew, no inasina unuma me unufan.
clean.tl: You have no say, you did not call the spirit name.

clean.tx: Uferap nainiw burir aawep woosa arufeya waaya nain inek.
clean.tl: He missed and again took an axe and when he hit it in the head the pig fell.

clean.tx: Ineya yena ikiwemi nainiw woowa erup arowamkun iiwawun umok.
clean.tl: It fell and I myself went and speared it again twice and it died altogether.

clean.tx: Umeya merena ereerup ifara aawep kaikap nabena suuwap akua aawep orom.
clean.tl: It died, and having taken a vine I tied its legs two and two and pushed it onto a carrying pole and carried it on my shoulder and came down.

clean.tx: Oromikok Pauli ame era wia urufap Pauli ikos waaya nain akua aawemik.
clean.tl: Coming down I saw Pauli and others on the road and I carried it with Pauli on our shoulders.
We carried it on our shoulders and came down to the village.

clean.tx: Urera waaya gelemuta nain paep, kiokiowa naap aawep uupep enemik.
clean.tl: In the afternoon we butchered the small pig, took the pieces like that, cooked and ate.

clean.tx: Yiena iisow yiena garanga muutiw aawep uupep enemik.
clean.tl: Just our family by ourselves took and cooked and ate it.
The talk is only like that, it is finished.

clean.tx: Mua nain ona emeria onaria ikua, ne mua nain urema osarena ikiwok.
clean.tl: There was that man with his wife, and the man went to hunt bandicoots.

clean.tx: Naap maakeya aria ona womar emeria nain kukusa nain miimak.
clean.tl: When she told her like that alright the spirit of his lady friend heard that.

clean.tx: Miimap ikiwok, ikiwep mua nain urema osarena iimarep ikeya ona mua nain ifakimok.
clean.tl: She heard it and went; she went and, as the man was standing on the bandicoot path, killed his man.
She killed him and as he was dead she was crying.

clean.tx: Sawur emeria nain ona soma mua nain ifakimok.
clean.tl: The spirit woman killed her lover.

clean.tx: A naap maemi omome na, ‘Mua yii, mua yee.’
clean.tl: Cry like that, Man yii, man yee.
They told her like that.

clean.tx: Ne mauwa nain aawep iima wuomap omemikua, sawur emeria nain
clean.tl: And she took this thing whatever and put it on his chest and cried, the spirit woman .
As she was crying and crying it dawned.

clean.tx: Epa wiimeya sawur emeria nain ikiweya, o iikirami owowa ekapok.
clean.tl: When it dawned and the spirit woman went, he got up and came to the village.
The story is like that.

clean.tx: Yiena emeria mia damolalimik nain mia aka nain aawep pikiwep manina upuna wuak, mia aka nain aawep.
clean.tl: We women have menstruation took that menstrual blood and took it to the garden and put it in a furrow, having taken that menstrual blood.
When she put it in the furrow both a son and a daughter appeared.

clean.tx: Ne onak aaya wia aawomaya enimoromikemik.
clean.tl: And their mother got sugarcane for them and they went down eating it.
They went down to the village with their mother.

clean.tx: Owowa orop owowa onak maa uupok.
clean.tl: They went down to the village and in the village their mother cooked food.

clean.tx: Maa uupep fofola urupeya maa opiya iiwok.
clean.tl: She cooked the food and it boiled and was done and she dished it out.

clean.tx: Maa pikiwomiwkin wiawi wia mokakurupok wia mokakorok, “I muuka marew a, wiipa marew a”, naap wia maakek.
clean.tl: When they took food to him, their father stared them up and down, “We have no son, no daughter,” he told them.

clean.tx: Ne wiawi maa nain aawemi mia iinan wiar sawikak.
clean.tl: And taking the food their father poured it on them.
Crying they told her .
And then they slept.
They said and their mother rolled string for them.

clean.tx: Wia kemie kemie kemie kemuka nain maayarek.
clean.tl: She rolled and rolled and rolled it them and the string became long.
It became long and she told it to them.

clean.tx: “Ae, aite, i uurika oraiyan, ifera unowa oraiyan.”
clean.tl: Yes, mother, tomorrow we’ll go down, we’ll go down to fetch saltwater.
Oh, fetch it right there.
No, we’ll go right down.
They held onto the string and went down.

clean.tx: Ne kemuka nain pepekereya onak ona wiar puukak.
clean.tl: And when the string was long enough their mother herself cut it.

clean.tx: Puukeya wi erup nain onoma oromik.
clean.tl: She cut it and the two of them went down to the horizon.
Alright when it dawned the sun rose.
The sun rose and burned their father.

clean.tx: Wiawi kuumeya, kuumeya, kuumeya awep eka iwak na wia, eka saanare
clean.tl: It burned and burned and burned their father and when he burned he went into a river but no, the river dried.

clean.tx: Eka oko iwak na wia, eka oko saanare
clean.tl: He went into another river but no, the other river dried.

clean.tx: Ne wiawi kuumeya kuumeya umok, ama kuumeya.
clean.tl: And when it burned and burned their father he died; when the sun burned him.

clean.tx: Yo aakisa iwera mauwowa nain maiyem.
clean.tl: Now I talk about coconut work.

clean.tx: Kiikir akena iwera opa aawep upimik.
clean.tl: First of all we get coconut seedlings and plant them.

clean.tx: Upep mokoma ikur naap ikiweya makenariya.
clean.tl: We plant them and when about five years have gone they bear fruit.

clean.tx: Iwera makenarep ififa wuaiya, ne ififa oraeya fiirimimik.
clean.tl: Coconut bear fruit and develop dry coconuts, and when dry coconuts drop we gather them.

clean.tx: Emeria fiirimikiwep aria ikoka mua kaisimik.
clean.tl: The women have go around and gather them, alright later the men husk them.

clean.tx: Mua kaisap neeke wuap miiwaasa nopap miiwaasa iwer ififa nain aawep pekapep epia koora mamaiya wueya fookimik.
clean.tl: Men husk them and leave them there and look for a truck, and when the truck takes the dry coconuts and brings them and puts them close to the to the drying shed we split them.
We split them and take them up and put them in the shed.

clean.tx: Koora wuap weesereya uurikona epia wuaimik.
clean.tl: When we put them in the shed and it is finished, the following day we light the fire.

clean.tx: Epia wuap ikiwep iwera kuufamikeya iwera reeneya iwer urupa anumimik.
clean.tl: We light the fire and go and watches the coconuts, and when the coconuts have dried we knock the coconut shells.

clean.tx: Iwer urupa anumap weesereya porop, owaruma porop mikimik.
clean.tl: We knock the coconut shells and when that is finished we take it down, we take it down outside and hit it .

clean.tx: Mikap weesereya owow maneka sesekap maamuma aawimik.
clean.tl: We hit it and when it is finished we send it to town and get money.
Now the talk is only like that, it is finished.

clean.tx: Yo aakisa manina uuwowa opora mainen naep.
clean.tl: Now I want to talk about garden work.
First of all the women clear the bush for the garden.

clean.tx: Nopap weesereya mua ikiwep nomokowa warimik.
clean.tl: When they have finished clearing the bush the men go and cut the trees.

clean.tx: Nomokowa warep oromakeya naap ikok nomokowa reeneya saama kuumimik.
clean.tl: When they have cut the many trees down and they have stayed like that and the trees have dried they burn the cleared bush.
When they have finished burning the cleared bush they burn the unburnt wood.
They burn the unburnt wood and split the garden into sections.
They split the sections and when it is finished they raise the planting sticks .

clean.tx: Weria fakerap mua unowa wiinariwkin emeria uupura upimik.
clean.tl: They raise the planting sticks and many men make planting holes and women plant taro seedlings.

clean.tx: Moma nan miiwa ikok siiwa erepam ikur naap moma pareweya perekimik.
clean.tl: The taro is there in the ground and in about four or five months it matures and is harvested.
And we make two gardens.
Big garden and small garden.

clean.tx: Manin maneka unuma ekina, aria manin gelemuta unuma esewa.
clean.tl: The name of the big garden is ekina’, the name of the small garden is ‘esewa.

clean.tx: Esewa naap: mua kuisow erup, arow, naap onimik.
clean.tl: ‘Esewa’ is like that: one man two three, we do like that.

clean.tx: Aria manin maneka, ekina, pun naap: mua kuisow manina erup arow naap.
clean.tl: Alright the big garden, ‘ekina’, is also like that: one man two or three, like that.

clean.tx: Ne manin gelemutitik, esewa, nena kookalowa perekinan.
clean.tl: And the small gardens, ‘esewas’, you will harvest at your own liking.
You watch it yourself, it will mature, you may harvest it.

clean.tx: Manin maneka, ekina, naisow nena kookalowa perekowa weetak.
clean.tl: you are not allowed to harvest the big garden, ‘ekina’, by yourself at your own liking.

clean.tx: Nena owowa onaiya aakunep perekowa ikua.
clean.tl: The harvesting must take place after you have talked with your village.

clean.tx: Waaya ikainon waaya uupinan naap, e owowa oko wienakowa pun naap, nena waaya ikok eliw wienakinan.
clean.tl: If you have a pig, you will cook pork, like that; or giving food to other villages is also like that: when you have a pig you may feed them.

clean.tl: We are secluded there in the house and have locked the door on ourselves and eat roasted bananas and taros.

clean.tx: Eka me enimimik, iwera eka me enimimik.
clean.tl: We don’t drink water, we don’t drink coconut water.

clean.tx: Nain enemikok inimik, kokomariya, inimik, epa wiimiya.
clean.tl: We eat that and sleep, it becomes dark, we sleep, it dawns.

We stay there.

clean.tx: Yia naeya, fofa yia wuomeya i yakimik.
clean.tl: When she says so about us and sets the date for us we bathe.

clean.tx: Yaki urupemi koora nan pokap ikaimik.

clean.tx: Sosora aimik, aite fia yia awomimik, ofa opimik, epa maneka oraimik.
clean.tl: We tie a grass skirt on, our mothers shave our hair, we are painted with red dye and we go down to the open.

clean.tx: Epa maneka orop maa ikina ewur me enimimik, mera eka.
clean.tl: We go down to the open but we do not eat meaty food soon, or fish soup.

clean.tx: Nan ikaimik, nan ikok, siiwa oko kerereya i maa ikina enimimik.
clean.tl: We stay there, we stay there and when another moon appears we eat meaty food.

clean.tx: Aite maimik, “No aakisa maa ikina enime”, a i maa ikina enimimik.
clean.tl: Our mothers say, “Now eat meaty food”, so we eat meaty food.

clean.tx: A weeserek, i maa momor enimiyen, waaya, maa mauwa, aara, nepa enimimik.
clean.tl: It is finished, and we eat any food, we eat pork, whatever, chicken, birds.

clean.tx: I ikoka ikoka wia, maa momor enimiyen.
clean.tl: Not sometime in the future, we eat food indiscriminately.

clean.tx: I naap onimik, i sira. Weeserek.
clean.tl: We do like that, it is our custom.

clean.tx: I mua soopowa sira, i yiena kae sira, kome sira, a naap, i wiipa mauwa sira saarik.
clean.tl: Our custom of burying our husbands – our grandfathers custom, our grandmothers’ custom – is like that, similar to the custom of our daughters’ what custom.

clean.tx: I mua umiya, mua omep omep omep mua napuma yiar soopimik.
clean.tl: When the husband dies we cry and cry and cry and the man’s body is buried.
It is taken and put in the grave.

clean.tx: Eruwa wia wuaiwkin i emeria apura yiena mua weria emeria nain yia amapikiwep eka yia yakuwap ekapemi koora yia wuaimik.
clean.tl: It is put in the grave and we widows are taken by our weria-relatives wives and washed in a spring and brought and put in the house.

clean.tx: Yiena koora yia wuaiwkin naap yiena koora nan ikaimik.
clean.tl: They put us in the house and we stay there in our house like that.
We stay secluded there in the house.

clean.tx: Ikok ikok moma ikowa enemikok, siiwa kuisow.
clean.tl: We stay and stay and keep eating roasted taro one month .

clean.tx: A yakimik, yiena mua weria emeria yookap eriwkin yakimik.
clean.tl: So we bathe, our weria-relatives wives follow us and we bathe.

clean.tx: Erap eka damola yakiep sosora aimik, maa bala suuwimik, kamukamu, kululuma, sagat.
clean.tl: We go and bathe in the bad spring and tie the grass skirt on and put on decorations, Job’s tears, coloured beads and sagat shells.

clean.tx: Fia yia awomiwkin ofa, irap owowa yiena koora
clean.tl: When they have shaved our heads we red dye – having come back – in the village, in our house.

clean.tx: Yiena koora opap, maa piep, saasaria piep owowa uruma oraimik.
clean.tl: In our house we put on , stick things in the armbands, stick saasaria plant in the armbands and go down in the open.

clean.tx: Oromkun mua weria meta urupa opap keemamuuna, umakuna meta yia mikimik.
clean.tl: We go down and the weria-relatives hold the meta-paste cup and stick the meta paste on our knees and on the neck.

clean.tx: Meta yia mikiwkin mera, waaya, oposia tiira nain yia aawomiwkin furunimik.
clean.tl: They1 stick the meta paste on us and when they2 get fish and pork, pieces of those meats for us they1 spit it.

clean.tx: Ama urupowa, ama orowa furunimik, koora ikiwimik.
clean.tl: They spit it towards east, they spit it towards west, and we go into the house.

clean.tx: Koora ikiwimik nain mera eka me enimimik.
clean.tl: We who go into the house do not eat fish soup.

clean.tx: Mera eka enowa marew nan ikaimik.
clean.tl: We stay there without eating fish soup.

clean.tx: Mera eka enowa marew ikok ikok mua weria maiya, “No aakisa maa ikina enime.”
clean.tl: We stay and stay without eating fish soup and a weria-relative says, Now you eat meaty food.

clean.tx: Ne maa ikina enimimik, mera eka enimimik.
clean.tl: And we eat meaty food, we eat fish soup.

clean.tx: Mera eka enimimik nain i mangala me enimimik, waaya me enimimik, mua wia soopimik nain.
clean.tl: We eat fish soup but we we do not eat drupa shells, we do not eat pork, we who bury our husbands.

clean.tx: A i sira, aria nepa me enimimik, aara me enimimik, maroka me enimimik, sibaur me enimimik.
clean.tl: Oh that is our custom, alright we do not eat bird meat, we do not eat chicken, we do not eat prawns, we do not eat lobsters.
We do not eat drupa shell soup.

clean.tx: Emi kekanowa maneka, naap oram ikaimik.
clean.tl: It is a big taboo, we stay like that just .

clean.tx: I ikoka nain enimiyen mua kukusa mia yia damoliwkin i eliwa me ikaiyen.
clean.tl: If we later eat that our husbands spirits will damage our bodies and we will not be well.
Our bodies will shrink and we will be like old people.

clean.tx: I sira naap yiar ik i mua soopowa sira, i emeria sira
clean.tl: We have a custom like that, the custom of burying our husbands, it is the womens custom.

clean.tx: Aria i emeria sira nan weesere
clean.tl: Alright the women’s custom is finished.

clean.tx: A pun naap, mua emeria umimik wi koora nan ikaimik.
clean.tl: Also in the same way, the men’s wives die and they stay there in the house.

clean.tx: Onak moma wia ikemikomimik, maa muutumut, akia, iwoka.
clean.tl: Their mothers roast taro for them, and all kinds of food, banana, yam.

clean.tx: Wia ikomiwkin enemikaiwkin enemikaiwkin siiwa kuisow, koora nan ikaimik nain.
clean.tl: They1 roast it for them2 and they2 keep eating it a month , those who stay there in the house.

clean.tl: The weria-relatives come and stay in the house and bring the son down.
They bring the son down and take him and he bathes.
They wash him in the water and bring him .
They bring him and the custom like that, similar to the women.

clean.tx: Mera eka me ewur enimiya, nan ikaiya, eka enemikainon.
clean.tl: He does not eat fish soup soon, he stays there, he will eat with water.

clean.tx: Maa eka enep enep siiwa ara onaria, maa ikina, mangala wia, waaya wia, aara wia, urema wia, maroka wia, maa muutumut wia.
clean.tl: He will keep eating food with water until the moon is right, no meaty food, drupa shell, no pork, no chicken, no bandicoot, no prawns; all kinds of food are forbidden.

clean.tx: Ikoka ona mua weria wia opomiwkin eniminon.
clean.tl: Later when his weria-relatives hold them for him he will eat them.

clean.tx: A wi mua sira emeria soopowa sira, wi mua era
clean.tl: That is the men’s custom, the custom of burying one’s wife, the way of the men.
There’s the talk.
It is finished.

clean.tx: Yo aakisa ifer maneka urupiya nain maiyem.
clean.tl: Now I tell about a tidal wave .

clean.tx: Yo me baliwep paayarem, oram iperowa nanariwkin miimam.
clean.tl: I do not understand it well, I have just heard the elders tell stories about it.

clean.tx: Kiikir akena menat maneka goronep oraiya.
clean.tl: First of all the big tide goes very low down.

clean.tx: Goronep oraiya nain, mua pepena menat ekiya naep menat orainan.
clean.tl: When it goes low down, an ignorant man thinks that the ebb tide is receding and will go down .
the knowledgeable people run away.

clean.tx: Ae, menat maneka goronep oraiya nain orop, malol.
clean.tl: Yes, the big tide that goes down, goes down the deep sea.

clean.tx: Suuwurupep urupep owowa erepura nan nainiw goronep oraiya.
clean.tl: It pushes up and rises and from the side of the village it goes down again.

clean.tx: Goronep oraiya nain maa muutitik iiwawun lalatiya.
clean.tl: When it goes down it washes away everything.

clean.tx: Koora e maa mauwa nain iiwawun samoriya.
clean.tl: It completely destroys houses or whatever.

clean.tx: Ne mua baurarep ikiwep koka ikaimik.
clean.tl: And people run away and stay in the jungle.

clean.tx: Aakisa fan ifera goron oreya wi owowa oraimik.
clean.tl: Only when the sea has receded they come down to the village.

clean.tx: Owowa orop owowa kuufimik na owowa iiwawun samorarek, ifera samorak.
clean.tl: They come down to the village and look at the village – it is completely destroyed; it is the sea that has destroyed it.

clean.tx: Ne ifera suuwiya nain koora pun iiwawun muiya.
clean.tl: And when the sea pushes up it completely swallows the houses.

clean.tx: O no mua me baurarinan nain ikoka ifera iiwawun nefa ifakiminon.
clean.tl: You who do not run away will later be completely killed by the sea.
